doc.title: Al Tinney interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Leaving the jazz scene for commercial work
summary: Tired of drugs and competitive cutting at Monroe's, he went commercial and played shows in Greenwich Village.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: We haven’t talked much about what society music was at the time. Now you got kind of disillusioned with the narcotic scene and so forth. And did you consciously say I’m going to get out of this?
You had enough self preservation kind of?

Yeah. Well actually I had had enough jazz. I would more or less say that this influx of drugs and stuff was an excuse for me to get out, you know, to go commercial. I went commercial and played show tunes and things. And I played for shows in Greenwich Village. And I enjoyed that more than I enjoyed the jazz scene. Because there was none of this competitive thing going on. When I was at Monroe’s there was trumpet players trying to play higher than the other trumpets, or the saxophone player trying to play more notes. And you know it was like the axe cutting scene. And here we are at the piano playing behind these guys for like hours accompanying them for what they’re doing. So I got tired of it.
Yeah. You got a whole line of saxophone players waiting to sit in and you’re back there.
Oh man, some of them with the long throats that don’t know when to stop, you know? So that was it. That was a good excuse for me to get out of it.
